newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arab leaders have strong words on Israeli policy.
newsitem.headline: Arab leaders have strong words on Israeli policy.

text.p: Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak anchored crisis talks in Cairo on Thursday with Arab leaders who said Israel was killing off the Middle East peace process.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa, in one of the strongest statements on the crisis, said Israel could not expect to go on tricking the Arabs with fine-sounding promises.

Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri and Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara came to see Mubarak as a new row broke out in Israeli-Palestinian relations over an Israeli proposal to bypass interim withdrawals from the West Bank.
Israel has already angered Arab states by breaking ground on a Jewish housing or settlement project in East Jersualem.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat was expected in the afternoon and an Israeli spokeswoman said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would probably send his foreign policy adviser Dore Gold and possibly a foreign ministry official too.

Shara told a joint news conference with Moussa that he felt the Arab states were moving towards serious commitment to the Cairo summit agreement of last year. The summit made an implicit threat to suspend normal relations with Israel.

"Don't underestimate Arab intelligence and don't play games with us," Moussa added, addressing Israeli leaders. "We cannot be deceived with any shining and sugar-coated promises...the weight of which we know," he added.

The Egyptian minister said the Oslo agreement between Israel and the Palestinians clearly said the status of Jerusalem was for negotiation and that no one should take unilateral measures there -- an argument that the Israeli government rejects.

Israel considers Jerusalem -- the Arab eastern half of which was captured in the 1967 Middle East war -- to be its undivided capital. But Palestinians view the eastern part as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
"This means settlements and it means no steps in Jerusalem. No state will accept anything other than that. They have to understand that and that's what they will be told," he added.

"He (Netanyahu) is intelligent, no doubt, and we don't accuse him of being anything else. But we want him to have enough sensitivity and understand that he is not the only decision-maker," Moussa said.
Shara said: "Building the settlement in East Jerusalem is tangible proof that Netanyahu is not thinking of the peace process but of provoking the Arabs and the whole world.
Hariri, speaking after his meeting with Mubarak, reflected the Arab view that peace talks might not survive the crisis.
"It's clear that Israel is taking hardline positions, and these positions, in the Egyptian leadership's opinion and ours, will help to bury the peace process and kill it off," he said.
"The Arabs are in accord in refusing to accept Israeli policy, in whole and in detail. Building settlements arouses Arab feelings and defies the world," he added.
Shara told reporters on arrival at Cairo airport that Egypt and Syria agreed the peace process was in crisis. Mubarak spoke to Syrian President Hafez al-Assad on Wednesday.
Shara also said another Arab summit might be necessary and consultations on this were under way.
But Hariri said Mubarak did not discuss an Arab summit and Moussa said there was no movement towards one.
Hariri added: "It's clear that Arab leaders agree that Israeli behaviour is threatening the peace process. But it doesn't necessarily take an Arab summit to solve the problem."
Mubarak has also made dire predictions about the Middle East peace talks because of the settlement dispute.

He said on Wednesday that Israel was leading the region back to violence. "If this settlement is built this will not be the end of the whole thing. It will be the beginning of a new era of violence which we would like to avoid," he said.
